notes:
Here are my research notes on Jeremiah 15, verse by verse. Some gaps first:

- **Not found:** I didn't reach any netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org notes. I found nothing from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org. Haydock's Catholic commentary is on studylight, but I didn't get to its text. I also found no prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter.
- **Partly read:** The Enduring Word (Guzik) page cut off at v. 16. My notes on vv. 16–21 come from other sources.
- **Labels:** Calling a writer "Reformed," "Baptist" and so on is my own shorthand. The pages themselves mostly don't name a tradition.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:** God had already told Jeremiah several times not to pray for the people. Here he says that even Moses and Samuel, great Old Testament intercessors, couldn't change Judah's fate. Several times before, God had told Jeremiah to *not* pray for the people, because their fate of judgment and exile was already certain (Jeremiah 7:16, 11:14, and 14:11). Adding to that previous thought, God said that even if two of the giants of the Old Testament – **Moses and Samuel** – were to intercede for Judah, it would not change their fate. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-15/
- Ellicott: "stood before Me" has a worship meaning, as in Jeremiah 35:19, picturing Moses and Samuel serving in the Temple courts. "stood before Him" (the phrase, as in Jeremiah 35:19, has a distinctly liturgical meaning), ministering in the Courts of the Temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/15-1.htm
- **Where traditions differ: do saints in heaven pray for us?** This is the clearest disagreement in the chapter, though all the sources I found are Protestant.
  - Calvin (Reformed) says Catholics wrongly used this verse to argue that dead saints pray for the living. He reads it as a hypothetical: *if* Moses and Samuel were alive. Moses and Samuel, they say, were dead, when God declared what is here said; it is then true that they prayed. There is here a supposition made, as though God did say, "If Moses and Samuel were now alive and interceded for them, I would yet remain implacable." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-15.html
  - Gill says the verse argues against the intercession of saints in heaven. this is against, and not for, the intercession of saints in heaven https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/15-1.htm
  - Matthew Henry agrees, and says the eternal Word (Christ) is the only Mediator in the next world. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/jeremiah-15.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary takes the quieter view that the verse simply isn't about that question. It is a mere supposition which is here made; there is no allusion to any popular view of the intercession of saints https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/15.htm
  - Note that I only have Calvin's hostile description of the Catholic view, not a Catholic source.
- **Application:** The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says there are limits to intercession. It adds that under grace, *Jesus can* do what Moses, Samuel and Jeremiah couldn't (Rom 8:3). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/jeremiah-15.html

**v. 2**
- Pulpit: The answer is a sternly ironical answer. Death, sword, famine, captivity, lie in wait for them in every possible road. "Death" here means "pestilence". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/15.htm
- Ellicott adds that "death" could possibly mean execution, but more likely pestilence. "Sword" means dying in a hopeless battle. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-15.html
- Guzik's summary: there would be no good ways to die. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-15/

**v. 3**
- Guzik: The four "destroyers" describe what happens to bodies after death. To an Israelite, having a corpse dragged off and left for animals was the worst possible desecration (he cites Feinberg). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-15/
- Pulpit: The sword applies to the living, and the other three to the unburied dead. "Drag away" is a better rendering than "tear." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/15.htm

**v. 4**
- Pulpit: "Make them a horror" (literally a *shuddering*) echoes the curses of Deuteronomy 28:25. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/15.htm
- Ellicott: The horror of that long and evil reign still lingered in the minds of men, and the prophet saw in it the beginning of the evils from which his people were now suffering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-15.html
- Guzik (citing Kidner): Manasseh was personally forgiven (2 Chron 33:12–13), but his legacy lived on in the sins he taught the people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-15/
- Pulpit (homiletics): Manasseh's crimes had never truly been repented of or forsaken. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-15.html

**v. 5**
- Pulpit: The horror onlookers feel will crowd out any pity. "Turn aside" pictures stopping in at someone's house. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/15.htm
- Kingcomments: Each question carries its own answer: no one. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/jeremiah-15.html

**v. 6**
- Pulpit: "I am weary of relenting" means God is tired of calling back his *conditional* sentence (see Jer 18:1–10). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/15.htm
- Ellicott: This is human language for God's patience, which is now used up. Perhaps, however, *I am weary of pitying* or *of relenting* would be a better rendering. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-15.html
- Guzik: Judah took God's restraint for granted. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-15/

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: The picture is the threshing floor and winnowing fork (Ps 1:4; Matt 3:12). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-15.html
- Pulpit: "Gates of the land" probably means the border fortresses rather than the cities in general. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/15.htm

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: The last line is better read as "travail-pangs and dismay." Translators were misled because the Aramaic word for labour pains is the same as the Hebrew word for "city." The Greek Old Testament (LXX) gets it right. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-15.html

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: Seven, the perfect number, stands for a complete family (1 Sam 2:5; Ruth 4:15). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-15.html
- Guzik (citing Feinberg): Seven sons pictured complete happiness, and hers ended too soon. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-15/

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: Verses 10–21 come in suddenly and may come from a later time. The commentary suggests the setting of Jeremiah 40, when Jeremiah chose to stay with Gedaliah, but admits this is uncertain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/15.htm
- Matthew Henry: Jeremiah wasn't someone who started fights. He was the one fought against, because he was faithful, and in this he is like Christ. not a man striving, but a man striven with; he was for peace, but, when he spoke, they were for war. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_015.cfm
- Ellicott: The cry to his mother shows his tenderness. Ellicott sees a "Mater dolorosa" (sorrowing mother) here, with a nod to Luke 2:35. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-15.html
- Constable reads it more severely: Since the Lord's call of him antedated his birth (Jeremiah 1:5), cursing his birth was tantamount to rejecting God's call on his life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/15-10.html
- Guzik quotes Spurgeon: it's harder to work *and wait* than simply to work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-15/

**v. 11**
- Pulpit: The Hebrew is hard. The KJV's "remnant" follows the Targum, the Vulgate and Rashi, but "I have loosed thee for good" may fit better. Rashi linked the verse to Nebuzaradan treating Jeremiah kindly (Jer 40:2–5). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/15.htm
- Ellicott: Better, *I will cause the enemy to be a suppliant to thee in time of evil.* Partial fulfilments of the promise are found in Jeremiah 21:1; Jeremiah 37:3; Jeremiah 42:2. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-15.html
- Guzik, citing Clarke, sees it fulfilled in Jeremiah 39:11. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-15/

**v. 12: two readings**
- Guzik: The "northern iron" is Babylon's weaponry, which Judah can't resist. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-15/
- Pulpit disagrees. Jeremiah wasn't thinking about Babylon breaking. The verse repeats God's promise that Jeremiah himself will be unbreakable (Jer 1:18–19), which leads into vv. 20–21. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/15.htm

**vv. 13–14**
- Pulpit: These verses suit the nation rather than Jeremiah and repeat Jeremiah 17:3–4. The commentary thinks they were probably copied in here by mistake. The Septuagint, Syriac, Targum and many manuscripts read "make thee serve thine enemies." "A fire is kindled" echoes Deuteronomy 32:22. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/15.htm
- Ellicott: Read where they stand, the words are addressed to Jeremiah as the people's representative. If the text has been moved, they belong with vv. 5–6. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-15.html

**v. 15: the prayer for vengeance**
- Ellicott compares it to the "vindictive" psalms (Pss 69, 109). He craves to see the righteous retribution for the sufferings which men have wrongfully inflicted on him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/15-15.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown says it isn't personal revenge. he speaks by inspiration God's will against the ungodly. Contrast in this the law with the gospel (Lu 23:34; Ac 7:60). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/15-15.htm
- Benson renders it "vindicate me." Gill allows it might partly come from Jeremiah's human frailty, since good people shouldn't seek private revenge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/15-15.htm
- Calvin: "Take me not away" means: while you are patient with this wicked people, don't let your wrath sweep me away. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/jeremiah-15.html
- Guzik (citing Thompson): For an Israelite, "remembering" means acting in the present, not just recalling. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-15/

**v. 16**
- Ellicott: The verse looks back to Jeremiah's call in chapter 1. Ezekiel 3:1–3 and Revelation 10:9 use the same image of eating God's words. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/15-16.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: The words became a joy because God's name was named on him, meaning God had chosen him to proclaim his word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jeremiah/15-16.htm
- Spurgeon (Baptist) divides the verse into the believer's secret life (feeding on the word) and public life (bearing God's name). https://www.preceptaustin.org/jeremiah_1516_commentary
- James Smith goes further and finds the living Word, Christ, in the verse. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60680/

**v. 17**
- Kingcomments: Jeremiah's separation wasn't the proud separation of a Pharisee. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kng/jeremiah-15.html

**v. 18: "like a mirage"**
- Barnes: The image is a brook that flows only in winter. Jeremiah had expected that there would be a perpetual interference of Providence in his behalf, instead whereof things seemed to take only their natural course. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/jps/jeremiah/15-18.html
- Bridgeway: Lonely and discouraged, Jeremiah feels that even God has failed him, like a thirsty man reaching a dried-up stream. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/15-19.html

**v. 19: did Jeremiah sin?**
- Ellicott: The prophet, like the people, must "return." He has to repent of his murmuring and distrust. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-15.html
- Constable: Jeremiah had been calling the people to repent, but he needed to repent of his self-pitying attitude. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/15-19.html
- Pulpit (homiletics) is gentler: Jeremiah was not plunged into grief through any unfaithfulness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/jeremiah-15.html
- Matthew Henry is in between. There was no cause to accuse Jeremiah of unfaithfulness, yet God saw fit to warn him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Jer/Jer_015.cfm
- On "they must turn to you": he must not copy the people. They must copy him (Bridgeway). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/jeremiah/15-19.html

**v. 20**
- Ellicott: The promise repeats the exact words of Jeremiah's call (Jer 1:18–19). It always depended on conditions, which the discouraged prophet had only partly kept. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-15.html
- Benson: Protection is renewed on condition of obedience. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/rbc/jeremiah-15.html

**v. 21**
- Pulpit: The "wicked" and "ruthless" may be the desperate bands who later murdered Gedaliah (Jer 41:1–3). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/15.htm
